en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes,
Section on the Donkey.
6. The Question on the Tortoise “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say that ‘five limbs of the tortoise are to be adopted,’ which are those five limbs to be adopted?
“Just as, Great King, the tortoise is a water-dweller who makes its home in the water alone;”
In the same way, great king, a practitioner of yoga, out of compassion for the welfare of all breathing beings and persons,
should dwell pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
“Great King, this is the first quality of the tortoise that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, when a tortoise is swimming in the water, if it raises its head and anyone sees it, it immediately submerges and dives deep, thinking, ‘Lest they see me again.

In the same way, Great King, when defilements descend upon him, a practitioner of yoga should submerge himself and dive deep into the lake of the meditation object, thinking, ‘Lest the defilements see me again.’”
This, great king, is the second quality of the tortoise that should be adopted.
Furthermore, great king, just as the tortoise, having emerged from the water, bakes its body in the sun;
even so, great king, the practitioner of yoga, having withdrawn the mind from sitting, standing, lying down, and walking, should bake the mind in the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).
This, great king, is the third quality of the tortoise that should be adopted.
Furthermore, great king, just as the tortoise digs into the earth and makes its dwelling in a secluded place,
even so, great king, the practitioner of yoga, having abandoned gain, honor, and fame, [should dwell] in an empty and secluded place.
Having entered a forest, a woodland thicket, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a place of little sound and little noise, secluded and remote,
one should take up residence in such solitude itself.
This, Great King, is the fourth quality of the tortoise that should be adopted.
This was said, Great King, by the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta:
“Secluded, free from noise,
frequented by wild beasts;”
"A bhikkhu should frequent a lodging for the sake of seclusion.
Furthermore, Great King, when a tortoise is wandering about, if it sees anyone or hears a sound...

Or, having placed his limbs— of which the trunk is the fifth— within his own skull, he stands quiet and indifferent, guarding the body; even so, Great King, the yogin, the practitioner of yoga, when forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles,
and mental phenomena assail him from all sides at the six sense doors, should not open the bolt of restraint, but should settle the mind within and maintain that restraint.
Having done so, one should dwell with mindfulness and clear comprehension, guarding the duty of a recluse.
This, Great King, is the fifth quality to be taken from the tortoise.
And this, Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One, the God above gods, in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya, in the Kummūpama Sutta:
“Just as a tortoise draws its limbs within its own shell,
let the bhikkhu withdraw his mental thoughts;
independent and not harming others, [let him dwell].”
“One who has attained final Nibbāna should not revile anyone.
Thus ends the sixth question, the Question on the Turtle.
